text: On November 21, 1915, a ship called Endurance sank in the Weddle Sea near Antarctica. All 28 men of her expedition were still alive, but they had no ship, no radio, and no way to tell the outside world where they were. They were stranded on drifting sea ice with three small lifeboats and whatever supplies they had managed to save. To get everyone home, six men would eventually have to cross more than 800 miles of open ocean in a boat barely seven meters long. The other 22 would have to wait, without knowing whether those six had survived. And even if the boat reached help, someone would still have to find a way back through the ice. In 1914, Ernest Shackleton set out to lead the first expedition across Antarctica, traveling from one coast to the other by way of the south pole. His ship, Endurance, was supposed to carry the expedition into the Weddle Sea where the crossing would begin. But in January 1915, moving pack ice closed around the vessel. For months, Captain Frank Warsley tracked their position while the crew maintained the ship and waited for a chance to escape. The sea ice moved with the winds and currents. Instead of carrying them toward their destination, it took the trapped ship wherever it drifted. Then, in October, the pressure became too great. The wooden hull began to give way. Water entered, and on October 27th, Shackleton ordered the men to abandon ship. They carried three lifeboats, provisions, and equipment onto the surrounding ice. On November 21st, Endurance sank. The expedition had never reached its starting point on the Antarctic continent. Now, the men had to find another way home. Shackleton first tried moving toward land on foot, but hauling heavy lifeboats across broken ice proved almost impossible. Ridges blocked their path, cracks forced detours, and the men made little progress. They abandoned the march and established a camp on a drifting flow. For months, they waited as the current carried them north. They rationed their food, hunted seals and penguins, and kept the lifeboats ready. In April 1916, the ice beneath them began breaking apart. On April 9th, they launched their boats into the water. For nearly a week, the crews rode and sailed between moving flows, struggling to reach Elephant Island. On April 15th, all 28 men finally landed. They had reached solid ground, but Elephant Island was uninhabited and far from normal shipping routes. No rescue ship knew they were there. Shackleton decided that a small crew must leave to find help. Their destination was South Georgia, roughly 1,300 kilometers, over 800 miles to the northeast across the Scotia Sea. There were whaling stations on the island. If the men could reach one, they could obtain help and organize a rescue. Their only suitable vessel was the largest lifeboat that James cared. The carpenter, Harry McNish, raised its sides, fitted a partial covering of wood and canvas, and worked to make the hull more watertight. Shackleton initially intended to leave Thomas Creen on Elephant Island to assist his second-in-command, Frank Wild. But after discussing the plan, he decided to take Creen on the ocean crossing instead. On April 24th, Shackleton departed with Worsley, McNish, Creen, Timothy McCarthy, and John Vincent. Twenty-two men remained under Wild's command. Wild's first challenge was finding shelter. An ice cave offered protection from the wind, but it was wet and unsuitable for living in. The men abandoned it. Instead, they built low stone walls and used two overturned lifeboats, canvas and other salvaged materials to form a roof. The shelter was cramped, but it gave the men somewhere to live as winter approached. While Wild organized life inside it, the James cared was already far out at sea. Finding South Georgia required more than sailing northeast. It was a small island in an enormous ocean. If the James cared passed too far to either side, the men might miss it entirely. Worsley had to navigate with a sextant, a compass, and calculations of their estimated progress. He needed the sun to determine their position. But cloud cover, heavy seas, and the constant movement of the boat made observations difficult. During the crossing, he obtained only four usable observations of the sun. Between them, he estimated their position from the course steered and distance traveled, adjusting whenever new evidence allowed. The others kept the boat moving and afloat. They worked in watches, handling the sails, steering, and bailing water. Ice accumulated on the vessel, adding weight that had to be removed. After nearly two weeks at sea, they were approaching where Worsley calculated South Georgia should be. On May 8th, land appeared through a break in the clouds. They had found the island. But heavy seas and dangerous surf prevented an immediate landing. For two more days, they remained offshore, searching for a safe approach. On May 10th, the six men finally landed in King Hawken Bay on South Georgia's western coast. The whaling stations were on the other side of the island. With the James Cared and its crew in their exhausted condition, attempting to reach those stations by sailing around the coast was too dangerous. Shackleton decided to cross the mountains instead. McNish, Vincent, and McCarthy remained behind. Shackleton, Worsley, and Creen set out on foot on May 19th. There was no established route through the mountains and glaciers. At one steep icy descent, Worsley and Creen held the rope while Shackleton used a carpenter's ads to cut steps into the ice. Descending roughly 500 feet took them about two hours. Then the three continued across snow fields and ridges, searching for a passage toward the inhabited coast. On May 20th, after approximately 36 hours of traveling, they reached the whaling station at Stromness. The three men left on South Georgia's western shore were subsequently brought to safety. But no news of any of this had reached Elephant Island. Wild and the other 21 men were still waiting. Inside their shelter, they maintained a daily routine, gathered food when they could, and endured the Antarctic winter without knowing whether the James Cared had reached its destination. Wild kept the group organized. Each day he rolled up his own sleeping bag, repeating that Shackleton might arrive that day. The others continued the work of maintaining the camp and finding food. Days passed. Then weeks. Shackleton's first rescue attempt aboard the whaling ship Southern Sky was stopped by pack ice. The next attempt, using the Uruguayan vessel Instituto de Pesca No. 1, and a later voyage aboard the schooner Emma, also failed to reach Elephant Island. Three attempts had failed, and the men on the island still had no news. As winter continued, food became increasingly scarce. By late August, the men were using what remained, and gathering limpets and seaweed along the shore. Shackleton secured a fourth opportunity. The Chilean government provided Yelcho, a small steam tug commanded by naval officer Luis Pardo. It was not an icebreaker. The ship could not force its way through a solid barrier of pack ice. On August 25th, Yelcho departed with Shackleton aboard. As the pack ice shifted toward the northeast, Shackleton chose to approach Elephant Island from the northwest. Pardo then had to bring the vessel safely through the waters near the island. In fog, he navigated among numerous grounded icebergs, guiding the small tug toward the camp. On August 30th, Yelcho reached Elephant Island. The men ashore were preparing food when a cry announced the approaching ship. At first, the words, ship-o were mistaken for lunch-o. Then, the men saw the vessel. After more than four months of isolation, a ship had reached their shore. Pardo brought Yelcho close enough for the evacuation to begin. All 22 men who had remained on Elephant Island were taken aboard. Every one of them was alive. The wider imperial transantarctic expedition had a different outcome. On the opposite side of Antarctica, the separate Ross Sea Party suffered its own ordeal, and three men died. The planned crossing of Antarctica was never completed. But the 22 men rescued from Elephant Island, together with the six who had sailed for help, accounted for every member of the Endurance Party. The expedition lost its ship. All 28 men came home alive.

They abandoned the march and established a camp on a drifting flow.
For months, they waited as the current carried them north.
They rationed their food, hunted seals and penguins, and kept the lifeboats ready.
In April 1916, the ice beneath them began breaking apart.
On April 9th, they launched their boats into the water.
For nearly a week, the crews rode and sailed between moving flows, struggling to reach Elephant Island.
On April 15th, all 28 men finally landed.
They had reached solid ground, but Elephant Island was uninhabited and far from normal shipping routes.
No rescue ship knew they were there.
Shackleton decided that a small crew must leave to find help.
Their destination was South Georgia, roughly 1,300 kilometers, over 800 miles to the northeast across the Scotia Sea.
There were whaling stations on the island.
If the men could reach one, they could obtain help and organize a rescue.
Their only suitable vessel was the largest lifeboat that James cared.
The carpenter, Harry McNish, raised its sides, fitted a partial covering of wood and canvas,
and worked to make the hull more watertight.
Shackleton initially intended to leave Thomas Creen on Elephant Island to assist his second-in-command, Frank Wild.
But after discussing the plan, he decided to take Creen on the ocean crossing instead.
On April 24th, Shackleton departed with Worsley, McNish, Creen, Timothy McCarthy, and John Vincent.
Twenty-two men remained under Wild's command.
Wild's first challenge was finding shelter.
An ice cave offered protection from the wind, but it was wet and unsuitable for living in.
The men abandoned it.
Instead, they built low stone walls and used two overturned lifeboats, canvas and other salvaged materials to form a roof.
The shelter was cramped, but it gave the men somewhere to live as winter approached.
While Wild organized life inside it, the James cared was already far out at sea.
Finding South Georgia required more than sailing northeast.
It was a small island in an enormous ocean.
If the James cared passed too far to either side, the men might miss it entirely.
Worsley had to navigate with a sextant, a compass, and calculations of their estimated progress.
He needed the sun to determine their position.
But cloud cover, heavy seas, and the constant movement of the boat made observations difficult.
During the crossing, he obtained only four usable observations of the sun.
Between them, he estimated their position from the course steered and distance traveled, adjusting whenever new evidence allowed.
The others kept the boat moving and afloat.
They worked in watches, handling the sails, steering, and bailing water.
Ice accumulated on the vessel, adding weight that had to be removed.
After nearly two weeks at sea, they were approaching where Worsley calculated South Georgia should be.
On May 8th, land appeared through a break in the clouds.
They had found the island.
But heavy seas and dangerous surf prevented an immediate landing.
For two more days, they remained offshore, searching for a safe approach.
On May 10th, the six men finally landed in King Hawken Bay on South Georgia's western coast.
The whaling stations were on the other side of the island.
With the James Cared and its crew in their exhausted condition, attempting to reach those stations by sailing around the coast was too dangerous.
Shackleton decided to cross the mountains instead.
McNish, Vincent, and McCarthy remained behind.
Shackleton, Worsley, and Creen set out on foot on May 19th.
There was no established route through the mountains and glaciers.
At one steep icy descent, Worsley and Creen held the rope while Shackleton used a carpenter's ads to cut steps into the ice.
Descending roughly 500 feet took them about two hours.
Then the three continued across snow fields and ridges, searching for a passage toward the inhabited coast.
On May 20th, after approximately 36 hours of traveling, they reached the whaling station at Stromness.
The three men left on South Georgia's western shore were subsequently brought to safety.
But no news of any of this had reached Elephant Island.
Wild and the other 21 men were still waiting.
Inside their shelter, they maintained a daily routine, gathered food when they could, and endured the Antarctic winter without knowing whether the James Cared had reached its destination.
Wild kept the group organized.
Each day he rolled up his own sleeping bag, repeating that Shackleton might arrive that day.
The others continued the work of maintaining the camp and finding food.
Days passed.
Then weeks.
Shackleton's first rescue attempt aboard the whaling ship Southern Sky was stopped by pack ice.
The next attempt, using the Uruguayan vessel Instituto de Pesca No. 1, and a later voyage aboard the schooner Emma, also failed to reach Elephant Island.
Three attempts had failed, and the men on the island still had no news.
As winter continued, food became increasingly scarce.
By late August, the men were using what remained, and gathering limpets and seaweed along the shore.
Shackleton secured a fourth opportunity.
The Chilean government provided Yelcho, a small steam tug commanded by naval officer Luis Pardo.
It was not an icebreaker.
The ship could not force its way through a solid barrier of pack ice.
On August 25th, Yelcho departed with Shackleton aboard.
As the pack ice shifted toward the northeast, Shackleton chose to approach Elephant Island from the northwest.
Pardo then had to bring the vessel safely through the waters near the island.
In fog, he navigated among numerous grounded icebergs, guiding the small tug toward the camp.
On August 30th, Yelcho reached Elephant Island.
The men ashore were preparing food when a cry announced the approaching ship.
At first, the words, ship-o were mistaken for lunch-o.
Then, the men saw the vessel.
After more than four months of isolation, a ship had reached their shore.
Pardo brought Yelcho close enough for the evacuation to begin.
All 22 men who had remained on Elephant Island were taken aboard.
Every one of them was alive.
The wider imperial transantarctic expedition had a different outcome.
On the opposite side of Antarctica, the separate Ross Sea Party suffered its own ordeal, and three men died.
The planned crossing of Antarctica was never completed.
But the 22 men rescued from Elephant Island, together with the six who had sailed for help,
accounted for every member of the Endurance Party.
The expedition lost its ship.
All 28 men came home alive.
